name: Differential-roller drafting for spinning
summary: Pairs of rollers turning at different speeds stretched loose fibre into a thin strand for spinning, letting machines replace skilled hands in Arkwright's mills.
description: Successive gripping rollers turn at different surface speeds to draw a supplied bundle of textile fibres into a thinner, longer strand for spinning.
tier_reason: A major reusable result, process or system within its field; broader multi-field or multi-generation dependence on this exact referent is not established.

impact.note: Spinning was reorganised around roller drafting, its yarn reached many societies, and the line of spinning machinery grew from it.

market.note: The capability can be used in economic production; this does not establish a first offer or sale.

date.label: by 1772
date.basis: A modern historian reports that the Nottingham mill was in full production in late 1772; machine-specific application of the 1769 patent is a scoped inference.

events.statement: Arkwright’s Nottingham spinning mill was in full production by the end of 1772; the differential-roller configuration of its frames is inferred from his 1769 specification.
events.scope: Spinning frames using successive roller pairs at different surface speeds, as described in Arkwright’s 1769 specification, inferred at his Nottingham production mill.
events.population: Workers at Arkwright’s Nottingham spinning mill
events.caveats: The 1738 Paul patent described differential roller pairs and an alternative. Styles links the drafting-roller design to the Northampton machines used from 1743; Seymour-Jones argues the operative Paul–Wyatt machines used the spindle-drawing alternative, while Bates notes that none survive and the evidence is sparse. Their exact earlier configuration is disputed. Earlier use of Arkwright’s rollers is also possible. The Nottingham account does not inventory each machine, so application of the 1769 specification is an inference. No first-global-use or first-commercial-sale claim is made.
